question: In population-based cohorts of older adults, which operationalisation of MCI gives the more stable diagnosis over follow-up (the lower proportion reverting to normal cognition): conventional/Petersen criteria (one test about 1.5 SD below the norm plus complaint) or neuropsychological Jak/Bondi criteria (two tests 1 SD below the norm in a domain)? P-986 answers in GAS/SNAC (Sweden, random population samples aged 60+), P-1136 in InveCe.Ab (Italy, population-based, aged 70-74 at baseline). Same population class (community older adults), same channel (neuropsychological tests with algorithmic criteria). P-1136 itself presents its result against P-986's ('Previous research ... has shown contrasting results. Overton and colleagues reported ... similar reversion rates').
metric: Proportion reverting to normal cognition among MCI cases followed up, computed as reverters / (reverters + stable), compared between the two criteria. P-986 prints it. For P-1136 it follows exactly from its printed consistency, because non-uncertain cases are either consistent or reverters. It is also derived from P-1136's Table 3 counts. One definitional difference remains: P-1136 counts dementia progressors as consistent, while P-986 removes progressors. It is tested below.

figures.P-986: Reversion, Petersen against modified NP (complaint kept): 323/744 = 43.4% (39.8-47.0) against 181/375 = 48.3% (43.2-53.5), printed. Petersen minus NP = -0.049. Assuming independent samples (conservative: the samples overlap, and positive correlation would narrow the SE), SE = sqrt(.434x.566/744 + .483x.517/375) = 0.0316, CI -0.111 to +0.013. Table 2 variants: follow-up requires impairment only, 42.1% (n 1063) against 45.3% (n 528), difference -0.031 (-0.083 to +0.021); impairment-only at baseline and follow-up, 43.3% (n 1579) against 45.3% (n 773), -0.020 (-0.062 to +0.023); original NP without complaint (P-1136's NP rule), 54.7% (50.4-59.0, n 528), so Petersen minus original NP = -0.113 (-0.169 to -0.058). Same-participant subsample (n = 334): Petersen 32.9% against NP 46.4%, difference -0.135, independence SE 0.0375, CI -0.209 to -0.062. In every version NP reverts as often or more often than Petersen.
figures.P-1136: Among the 280 diagnosed MCI under both criteria with non-uncertain status: consistent NP 177 (63.2%) against conventional 121 (43.2%), McNemar 32.9, p < 0.001 (printed). Reversion = 1 - consistency: conventional 159/280 = 56.8% (Wilson 0.509-0.625) against NP 103/280 = 36.8% (0.314-0.426). Discordant pairs from McNemar: continuity-corrected (|b-c|-1)^2/(b+c) = 32.9 with b - c = 177 - 121 = 56 gives b + c = 92 (b = 74, c = 18; 3025/92 = 32.88). Paired difference 0.200, SE = sqrt(92 - 56^2/280)/280 = 0.0321, CI 0.137 to 0.263 (b + c = 94 or 96 without the correction gives the same CI to 0.01). Full-sample Table 3: conventional reverters 192, consistent 133, so reversion 192/325 = 59.1% (0.537-0.643); NP reverters 246, consistent 285, so 246/531 = 46.3% (0.421-0.506). Conventional minus NP = +0.128 (independence SE 0.0348, CI +0.059 to +0.196).
figures.difference: Petersen minus NP reversion: P-986 between -0.02 and -0.135 across its analyses, with every upper bound at or below +0.023. P-1136 +0.128 (+0.059 to +0.196) in the full sample and +0.200 (+0.137 to +0.263) in the same-participant subsample. In every pairing each estimate lies outside the other's interval, and the directions are opposite. In the same-participant analyses, and against the original-NP rule, both directions are individually significant.

matched_figure_check: Several matched figures exist and none reconciles the pair. (1) NP rule: P-986 reports the original Jak/Bondi rule without complaint, the rule P-1136 uses. It gives 54.7% reversion against Petersen 43.4%, which widens the gap. (2) Same population subset: both papers report a same-participant analysis (P-986 n = 334, P-1136 n = 280), and they point in opposite directions (NP +13.5 points against NP -20.0 points in reversion). (3) Follow-up definition: P-986's relaxed follow-up requirements (Table 2: no complaint or ADL requirement at follow-up; impairment only) keep NP at or above Petersen. (4) Progressor handling: remove all incident-dementia cases from P-1136's Table 3 reverter and consistent counts to mimic P-986's exclusion of progressors. That gives conventional 172/262 = 65.6% against NP 237/449 = 52.8%, difference +0.129 (+0.055 to +0.202), so the ordering stays. This is approximate, because Table 3 counts incident dementia at any time, but it shows that the progressor rule does not remove the gap.

candidate_explanations.difference: Age window and cohort: InveCe.Ab enrolled one birth cohort aged 70-74 at baseline; GAS/SNAC pooled random population samples aged 60 to over 90.
candidate_explanations.quote: a population-based sample of older adults aged between 70 and 74 years of age at baseline and during 12 years of follow-up with periodic multidimensional assessment

candidate_explanations.difference: Prevalence of subjective complaints, which the conventional rule requires: probably low in P-1136's population sample, making conventional MCI rarer and possibly less persistent.
candidate_explanations.quote: Thus, the prevalence of subjective cognitive complaints in our sample was probably lower than that in the clinical setting, leading to a lower probability of being diagnosed with MCI on the basis of Conventional criteria.

candidate_explanations.difference: Education: low and heterogeneous in InveCe.Ab (mean 7.2 years), against the mostly well-educated cohorts P-1136 contrasts itself with.
candidate_explanations.quote: whereas our sample is highly heterogeneous in terms of educational level (see Table 6 for details) and is thus more representative of the aged population.

candidate_explanations.difference: Definition of stability: P-1136's 'consistent' requires meeting impairment criteria at every later wave and keeps progressors; P-986 follows each case to its first event and excludes progressors. The progressor part is approximately tested above and does not remove the gap.
candidate_explanations.quote: We considered consistent MCI those individuals who, once diagnosed, keep fulfilling the criteria for cognitive impairment in subsequent waves (regardless of dementia diagnosis)

candidate_explanations.difference: Reverter definition in P-986: complaint and intact ADL must persist, otherwise the case leaves the analysis rather than counting as a reverter. P-986's relaxed Table 2 variants keep the same ordering.
candidate_explanations.quote: Reverters were defined as participants that fulfilled all criteria for MCI, but no longer met the requirement for objective cognitive impairment, i.e., the participants had normal ADL, cognitive complaint, and no dementia

candidate_explanations.difference: Follow-up schedule and length: P-986 revisits every 3 or 6 years depending on age; P-1136 has waves over 12 years (0, 2, 4, 8, 12) with a change of internal normative sample at waves 4-5.
candidate_explanations.quote: Follow-up visits were made every third year for those older than 78 years and every sixth year for those younger than 78.

candidate_explanations.difference: Normative reference: external SNAC-Blekinge/Stockholm norms (7th/16th percentile) in P-986 against internal InveCe.Ab normative samples stratified by age and education in P-1136.
candidate_explanations.quote: Normative values were derived from two sister studies, SNAC-Blekinge and SNAC-Stockholm, which administrated the same cognitive tests in a standardized way

reason: Both papers compare the stability of Petersen/conventional against Jak/Bondi neuropsychological MCI criteria in community cohorts, and their orderings are opposite beyond uncertainty. In P-986, NP reverts as often or more often (up to +13.5 points in its same-participant analysis). In P-1136, conventional MCI reverts 12.8 points (full sample, +5.9 to +19.6) to 20 points (same participants, +13.7 to +26.3) more often. The papers' own matched figures, the original NP rule, the same-participant subsets, relaxed follow-up definitions and removal of progressors from P-1136's counts, all keep the gap. The age window, complaint prevalence, education, follow-up schedule and norms remain as candidate explanations. None is shown to be sufficient.

quotes.quote: Reversion rates were 323/744 (43.4%, 95% confidence intervals (CI): 39.8; 47.0) and 181/375 (48.3% 95% CI: 43.2; 53.5) for the Petersen criteria and NP criteria, respectively.
To calculate reversion rate, the proportion of reverters was compared to the proportion of non-reverters, i.e., the stable MCI group.
However, excluding cognitive complaint, as required in the original NP criteria, produced somewhat higher reversion rates (54.7%).

Previous research comparing the diagnostic stability of different MCI criteria has shown contrasting results. Overton and colleagues reported that Conventional and Neuropsychological criteria had similar reversion rates and diagnostic stability5.
We defined reverters as those who, after MCI diagnosis, were classified as cognitively normal in subsequent waves.
